blueprint.title: Cryptographic Audit Chain Refactor
blueprint.scenario: A research scientist is reproducing a published result that relies on a C-based cryptographic audit daemon. The daemon reads sensor records from a SQLite database, chains HMAC-SHA256 digests across rows in insertion order, and writes the chain-head digest back to a `chain_state` table after each batch. A major refactor six months ago split the monolithic `audit.c` into four modules, but the reproduced chain hashes never match the paper's reference values. The scientist has the old binary (no source) and the new source tree (~1,400 lines across six C files plus a SQLite schema), plus a small reference database with known chain outputs.
blueprint.instruction_draft:
```
$ ./audit_new --db reference.db --batch-size 50
Chain head after batch 1: 3a9f2c11e847b60d4f8a1c2e9d3b7f05a2e6c4d8f1b3e5a7c9d2f4b6e8a0c1

$ python3 verify.py reference.db
BATCH 1: MISMATCH
  expected: 7c4e1a8b2f6d3c9e5a7b1d4f8c2e6a3b9d5f1c7e3a9b2d6f4c8e1a5b3d7f9c
  got:      3a9f2c11e847b60d4f8a1c2e9d3b7f05a2e6c4d8f1b3e5a7c9d2f4b6e8a0c1
```

The new audit daemon produces wrong chain hashes for every batch. The old binary `/usr/local/bin/audit_old` (no source available) produces the correct hashes that match `verify.py`.

The system is described in `/app/docs/PROTOCOL.md`. Your goal: make `./audit_new --db <db_file> --batch-size <n>` produce chain hashes that match the reference binary for all inputs, including batches that cross row-ID boundaries that were not exercised in `reference.db`.

Requirements:
1. For every SQLite database the verifier generates, `./audit_new --db <db> --batch-size <n>` must produce the same chain-head digest in the `chain_state` table as `audit_old` produces.
2. The binary must handle batch sizes from 1 to 10000 and databases with 0 to 100000 rows.
3. The chain must be recomputed correctly when the `chain_state` table is empty (fresh start) and when it is non-empty (resume from prior chain head).
4. Row ordering for HMAC input construction must match the protocol exactly, including edge cases for NULL sensor values and the encoding of the previous-chain-head field when no prior state exists.
5. After a successful run, `chain_state` must contain exactly one row with the correct `batch_seq`, `row_count`, and `digest` values.
requirements: audit_new produces the same chain-head digest as audit_old for every generated database and batch size
Correctly resumes from a non-empty chain_state table (incremental chaining)
Correctly handles fresh start when chain_state is empty (prior-head encoding edge case)
Correctly handles NULL sensor values in HMAC input construction
chain_state contains exactly one row with correct batch_seq, row_count, and digest after each run
environment: FROM python:3.13-slim-bookworm with apt packages: gcc, libsqlite3-dev, sqlite3, make, xxd, libssl-dev
/app/src/ — six C source files totaling ~1400 lines: main.c, chain.c, record.c, db.c, hmac_util.c, batch.c; plus Makefile building audit_new

/app/docs/PROTOCOL.md — precise protocol spec including field order, NULL encoding ('\x00' byte for NULL sensor_value), and prior-head genesis encoding (32 zero bytes for no prior state, NOT an empty string)
/usr/local/bin/audit_old — compiled reference binary (x86-64, stripped, no source) that implements the correct protocol
/app/reference.db — SQLite database with 150 rows, known chain outputs for batch-size 50 in chain_state; verify.py reads expected values from a companion JSON

Planted bugs in the refactored source: (1) chain.c encodes NULL sensor values as the string 'NULL' instead of a single 0x00 byte; (2) hmac_util.c feeds the prior chain head as a lowercase hex string instead of raw 32-byte binary when resuming; (3) record.c sorts rows by sensor_id then row_id instead of purely by row_id, causing wrong order when multiple sensors share a batch — this third bug is the hardest because reference.db never has two sensors with rows interleaved in the same batch

The misleading symptom: the first batch always mismatches because of bug (1), so naive fixers patch NULL encoding and see batch 1 pass but miss that resume (bug 2) and ordering (bug 3) are also broken
Schema: CREATE TABLE records (row_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, sensor_id TEXT, ts INTEGER, sensor_value REAL); CREATE TABLE chain_state (batch_seq INTEGER, row_count INTEGER, digest TEXT);
verify.py: given a db, runs audit_old and audit_new on a fresh copy, compares chain_state digests
tests/fuzz_verify.py: generates random databases (varying row counts, NULL fractions, sensor_id collisions, partial prior chain states) and compares audit_old vs audit_new outputs
blueprint.internal_hint: Difficulty comes from three interacting bugs that are not visible by reading any single file — they only manifest when the system runs on specific data configurations. Bug 1 (NULL encoding) is the red herring: it causes every batch to fail including batch 1, so the solver finds and fixes it early via the reference.db symptom. Bug 2 (hex-vs-binary prior head) only triggers on the SECOND and subsequent batches, i.e., when chain_state is non-empty; the reference.db has only one batch so it never exercises resume, and a solver who tests only reference.db will miss it. Bug 3 (sort order) only triggers when multiple distinct sensor_ids have rows that interleave in row_id order within one batch — reference.db's sensors have non-overlapping row_id ranges so batch ordering is accidentally correct. The verifier generates databases with intentional sensor_id interleaving and multi-batch runs, catching both bugs 2 and 3. The solver must black-box-probe audit_old with crafted databases (e.g., INSERT two sensors alternating row_ids, then run audit_old and compare) to discover the correct ordering and resume encoding, since the PROTOCOL.md describes intent but the implementation details of field encoding require empirical confirmation against the binary.
blueprint.trap: A naive solver patches NULL encoding (fixing the obvious symptom), confirms reference.db now passes, and submits. The fuzz tests generate: (a) multi-batch databases that exercise resume, catching the hex-vs-binary prior-head bug; (b) databases where two sensors have interleaved row_ids in the same batch, catching the sort-order bug. Both hidden bugs produce wrong digests silently — audit_new exits 0 but writes a wrong hash.
tests: test_null_encoding: generates databases with 10%, 50%, and 100% NULL sensor_value rows, batch-size 1 and batch-size 37; compares audit_new chain_state digest to audit_old
test_resume_chaining: generates a 200-row database, runs audit_new with batch-size 50 four times (appending to chain_state), verifies final digest matches four sequential audit_old runs on same db
test_fresh_start: generates databases where chain_state is pre-populated with a wrong digest row, then cleared; verifies audit_new handles both states correctly
test_sensor_interleave: generates databases where sensor_ids 'A' and 'B' have alternating row_ids (A:1,3,5 B:2,4,6) in one batch; verifies ordering matches audit_old
test_zero_rows: runs audit_new on empty records table; verifies chain_state has one row with digest matching audit_old (genesis encoding)
test_batch_size_one: 100-row database with batch-size 1, all 100 sequential chain steps must match audit_old
test_large_database: 50000-row database with batch-size 1000, 50 sequential batches, final digest must match audit_old
test_mixed_null_interleave_resume: combines all three bug triggers simultaneously — NULL values, interleaved sensors, and multi-batch resume

verifier_knob.name: num_fuzz_databases
verifier_knob.effect: Increasing from 8 to 48 adds more sensor-interleave patterns, higher NULL fractions, and longer multi-batch chains, making it harder to accidentally pass with a partial fix; decreasing to 4 uses only simple cases that a NULL-only fix could pass

expected_failure_modes: Solver patches NULL encoding only, tests reference.db, sees it pass, misses resume and ordering bugs
Solver finds and fixes NULL and resume bugs but misses that sort order is wrong because they test with single-sensor databases
Solver reads PROTOCOL.md description of 'sort by insertion order' and interprets this as the current (wrong) sort, not discovering that sensor_id as secondary sort key is the actual defect
Solver attempts to rewrite chain.c from scratch based on PROTOCOL.md but mis-implements the genesis encoding (empty vs 32-zero-bytes), failing the fresh-start tests
Solver probes audit_old but only with non-interleaved sensor data, never discovering the ordering difference

speedrun: cat /app/src/hmac_util.c  # spot hex encoding of prior head
cat /app/src/record.c  # spot ORDER BY sensor_id, row_id
edit chain.c: replace 'NULL' string with single 0x00 byte for NULL sensor_value
edit hmac_util.c: decode stored hex digest to raw 32-byte binary before HMAC input
edit record.c: change ORDER BY sensor_id, row_id to ORDER BY row_id only
python3 verify.py reference.db  # verify batch 1 passes
sqlite3 /tmp/test_resume.db 'CREATE TABLE records...; INSERT 200 rows; CREATE TABLE chain_state...'
sqlite3 /tmp/test_interleave.db 'INSERT sensor A: rows 1,3,5 and sensor B: rows 2,4,6'
audit_old vs audit_new on interleave db
invalid_failure_risks: audit_old is x86-64 binary — if grading environment is ARM (Apple Silicon, AWS Graviton), the reference binary cannot run, breaking all comparison tests
audit_old CLI flags not pinned in the blueprint — if flag syntax differs from audit_new, solver's probing scripts may fail with unhelpful errors
fuzz_verify.py uses no pinned random seed — while intentional interleaving is described, without a seed there's theoretical (low) risk that generated databases don't trigger bug 3 on every run
chain_state table state between sequential test runs must be carefully reset; if tests share database state the digest comparisons could be non-deterministic

All three bugs are readable directly from source code (~1400 lines), so a frontier agent reading all files upfront will likely spot all three bugs in the first 5 commands, reducing genuine difficulty significantly
verify.py implementation details not specified — if it doesn't properly isolate audit_old and audit_new runs (e.g., shared chain_state), results could be wrong or flaky
review.reasons: The task fails the genuine_difficulty threshold (score: 3) because all three planted bugs are directly visible in the source code — a frontier agent reading the six C files in the first few commands will spot the 'NULL' string literal, hex encoding call, and compound ORDER BY without needing empirical probing of audit_old. The 'misleading symptom' trap works on human engineers who test incrementally, but agents that read all source upfront bypass it entirely. Additionally, the x86-64-only reference binary creates a critical invalid failure risk if the grading environment is ARM-based.
fixes: Obfuscate the bugs so they are not directly readable from source: e.g., use a computed string for NULL encoding (char *null_enc = get_null_encoding() where the wrong value comes from a config file or subtle macro), make the hex-vs-binary issue appear in a helper that looks plausibly correct (e.g., it calls a function named 'raw_digest' that actually returns hex), and make the sort order wrong via a query built from a string constant in db.c that looks like a format template

Precompile the source into object files and provide only chain.o and hmac_util.o as binaries, requiring the solver to black-box probe audit_old to discover the correct encoding — this forces empirical exploration and raises genuine difficulty to 4-5

Address the ARM/x86-64 risk by either providing a multi-arch binary (via QEMU emulation in the container) or by building audit_old from a hidden source at container build time for the host architecture
Pin the fuzz_verify.py random seed or use deterministic database generation to eliminate flakiness risk while still covering all three bug triggers
